A pretense is a false show — it's when someone makes something appear to be true, real, or genuine when it actually isn't. Think of it as a mask worn over reality. The person is not being straightforward; instead, they are putting on a kind of performance to hide the truth or create a false impression.

The key word running through every meaning of "pretense" is falseness. Wherever you see the word, something fake is at play — a fake feeling, a fake reason, a fake identity, or a fake claim.

"Pretense" is a rich word that works in three closely related but slightly different ways:

Sense 1 — A False Act or Appearance

This is when someone behaves in a way that gives a false picture of how they truly feel or what is truly happening.

Example:

"Even though their marriage was falling apart, they kept up the pretense of being a happy couple in front of the children."

Here, "pretense" refers to the false act of happiness they were performing. The show on the outside did not match the reality on the inside.

More examples:

"She laughed along with everyone else, maintaining the pretense that she found it funny."
"He ate the terrible food with a smile, keeping up a pretense of enjoyment out of politeness."

In this sense, pretense is like a curtain drawn over reality.

Sense 2 — A False Reason Used to Do Something

This is when someone uses a made-up or misleading excuse as a cover story to do something. The stated reason is not the real reason.

Example:

"He knocked on her door under the pretense of asking for directions, but he really just wanted to see her."

The "asking for directions" part is the pretense — a fake reason that gets him in the door. The real reason is hidden behind it.

More examples:

"The company laid off employees under the pretense of 'restructuring,' but it was really just about cutting costs."
"She called him under the pretense of discussing work, though she really wanted to apologize."

This is also where the famous phrase "false pretenses" comes from — which means deceiving someone about your true identity, intentions, or reasons in order to get something from them.

"He obtained the money under false pretenses." (He tricked someone into giving him money by lying about who he was or why he needed it.)

Sense 3 — A False Claim to Having a Quality, Right, or Ability

In this sense, "pretense" refers to an undeserved or unjustified claim of possessing something — a skill, a status, a right, or a quality — that one doesn't truly have. This sense most commonly appears in negative constructions like "no pretense" or "without pretense."

Example:

"She is a good leader — someone without pretense, who never tries to seem more important than she is."

Here, "without pretense" means she makes no false claim of superiority or grandeur. She is genuine.

"He made no pretense of understanding the mathematics involved."

This means he did not falsely claim or act as if he understood it. He was honest about not knowing.

"The film made no pretense of being great art — it was simply made to entertain."

The film didn't try to falsely position itself as something deeper than it was.

To tie all three senses together: pretense always involves a gap between what is shown and what is real.

What is shown (the pretense)What is real
HappinessSadness
A friendly visitA hidden motive
ExpertiseIgnorance
ImportanceOrdinariness

"Keep up a pretense" — to continue maintaining a false appearance over time, often with some effort.

"For years, she kept up the pretense that everything was fine."

"Drop the pretense" / "Abandon the pretense" — to stop pretending; to let the false front fall away.

"Let's drop the pretense — we both know this partnership isn't working."

"Under the pretense of" — using something as a cover story.

"They entered the building under the pretense of making a delivery."

"Make no pretense of" — to not falsely claim or fake something.

"He makes no pretense of being a patient man." (He is openly impatient — he doesn't fake otherwise.)

"Without pretense" — genuine, unaffected, not trying to seem like something you're not.

"She spoke without pretense, and people trusted her for it."

"Pretense" is always negative in tone — it implies inauthenticity and dishonesty. However, the degree of moral judgment varies by context:

  • Sometimes it's serious deception — lying to gain money, access, or trust.
  • Sometimes it's lighter social pretending — being polite, keeping a secret to protect someone, or maintaining social harmony.

"They pretended not to know about the surprise party — a harmless pretense that made the evening magical."

So while pretense is always about falseness, it is not always sinister. Context tells you how heavily to judge it.

These two words are easy to confuse.

  • Pretense is the broader word — it covers any false act, false feeling, false claim, or false reason.
  • Pretext is narrower — it specifically means a false reason given to justify an action. It overlaps with Sense 2 of pretense, but that's all it does.

So every pretext is a kind of pretense, but not every pretense is a pretext.
Pretense is the art of making something false look true — whether it's a feeling, a reason, or a claim about yourself.
